content: A database connection leak occurs when application code checks out a connection from a pool but fails to return it on every teardown path. Typical signals include an increasing count of checked-out connections, a pool that remains exhausted after request load falls, database-dependent requests timing out, and temporary recovery after process restart. Diagnose by comparing pool checkout and checkin counts, inspecting long-lived sessions, and tracing cancellation, streaming, exception, and retry paths. Repair requires guaranteed cleanup in finally blocks or context managers, bounded pool timeouts, and alerts on sustained pool saturation rather than only database CPU.
title: Runbook: database connection leaks

content: A memory leak is sustained retention of memory that should have been released. Production symptoms often show resident memory rising across otherwise similar traffic windows, more frequent garbage collection, swap or OOM pressure, and recovery after restarting the leaking process. Investigation should compare heap growth with request volume, inspect retained object types, review caches and listener lifecycles, and distinguish a leak from an intentionally warm cache. Mitigations include bounding caches, removing stale references, closing resources, and deploying temporary restart protection while the retention path is fixed.
title: Runbook: memory leaks

content: Disk exhaustion occurs when a filesystem reaches capacity or inode limits and services can no longer create or extend required files. Common causes include unbounded logs, retained write-ahead logs, failed replication, temporary files, or runaway artifact generation. Signals include rapidly falling free space, write failures, database or queue errors, and recovery after space is freed or capacity is added. Diagnose the largest growth contributors and the process responsible before deleting data. Prevent recurrence with retention policies, replication health alerts, filesystem headroom alerts, and tested cleanup procedures.
title: Runbook: disk exhaustion

content: An N+1 query problem occurs when code fetches a collection and then performs an additional database query for each item. It appears as very high counts of similar single-row queries, latency increasing with list size, unnecessary network round trips, and database time dominated by repeated lookups. Confirm by tracing one request, grouping SQL by normalized statement, and comparing unbatched and batched call counts. Typical fixes are eager loading, joins, batch fetch APIs, prefetching, or restructuring the data-access layer so a list is resolved in a bounded number of queries.
title: Runbook: N+1 database queries

content: Payment incidents can be caused by configuration changes rather than payment-provider capacity. Indicators include failures beginning immediately after a rollout, a narrow card, region, gateway, or authentication segment being affected, normal infrastructure health, and recovery after reverting configuration. Investigation should compare the active configuration with the previous known-good version, check routing, 3DS, firewall, merchant, and entitlement rules, and correlate failure codes with the changed scope. Treat rollback as a mitigation and add validation, staged rollout, and configuration-diff observability before retrying the change.
title: Runbook: payment configuration failures

content: A no-fault classification is appropriate when investigation shows the observed symptom does not represent a production defect in the diagnosed service. Examples include stale dashboards, version skew in monitoring, expected maintenance behavior, upstream test traffic, or an alert whose assumptions are wrong. The diagnosis should be supported by independent health signals, request traces, deployment state, and reproduction attempts. Closing as no-fault should still record why the alert fired and whether observability or alert logic needs correction so the same false positive does not repeatedly consume incident response time.
title: Runbook: false alarms and no-fault incidents
